title: Abstract Classes (Abstrakte Klassen) and Interfaces (Schnittstellen)
summary: Abstract classes share state and common code, while subclasses make open methods concrete. `final` and `sealed` restrict inheritance and changes. Interfaces describe capabilities; their `default` methods can create inheritance conflicts, for which Java has fixed precedence rules.
keyFacts: An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly.
An abstract method has a signature but no method body.
A concrete subclass must implement all inherited abstract methods or itself be abstract.
Abstract classes may have instance fields and concrete methods.
In an expression tree, `getValue()` computes a value once and then stores it in the cache.
A separate `evaluated` field is needed because 0 can be a valid result.
For overridden instance methods, the object's runtime class determines which implementation runs.
`final` on a class prohibits subclasses; on a method it prohibits overriding; on a variable it prohibits reassignment.
A `final` reference does not prevent the referenced object from changing.
`sealed` with `permits` restricts the permitted direct subclasses.
A `switch` over a sealed hierarchy can omit `default` if all permitted cases are covered.
A class may have one direct superclass and implement multiple interfaces.
Interface methods without a body are implicitly `public abstract`; interface fields are `public static final` and must have an initializer.
For `compareTo`, a negative result means smaller, 0 means equal according to the ordering, and a positive result means larger.
Static interface methods are called through the interface name and are not inherited by implementing classes.
`Cloneable` is a marker interface and declares no `clone()` method.
For `default` conflicts, a concrete class method takes precedence over an interface default.
A more specific interface takes precedence over a more general inherited default; the class must resolve conflicts between unrelated defaults.

review.notes: Alle 45 Fragen geprüft. Behoben: ungültige Quellenverweise, fehlende Deklaration von y und mehrere hart codierte Verify-Antworten. Rechenwerte und Mermaid-Kontexte geprüft; keine Frage musste entfernt werden.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes an abstract class?

options.text: It can only be implemented by interfaces.
It may contain only abstract methods.
It can provide shared fields and methods but cannot be instantiated directly.
It can be instantiated directly as long as it has a constructor.

questions.explanation: An abstract class can combine state and finished code with open methods. Having a constructor does not make it directly instantiable.

questions.prompt: An abstract method has a signature but no ___.
questions.explanation: The declaration ends with a semicolon instead of a method body. The name, return type, and parameters make up the signature.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about `final`; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: A `final` array cannot contain modified elements.
A `final` variable cannot be reassigned after its initial assignment.

questions.explanation: `final` affects inheritance, overriding, or reassignment depending on where it appears. The elements of a final array reference can still be changed.

questions.prompt: With `final int[] a = {1};`, `a[0] = 2;` is prohibited because the reference is final.
questions.explanation: `final` only prevents `a` from being redirected to a different array here. The contents of the referenced array can still be changed.

questions.prompt: What does `permits` specify for a `sealed` class?

options.text: The interfaces a class must implement.
The methods that may not be overridden.

questions.explanation: `sealed` restricts inheritance. The `permits` list specifies which classes may inherit directly.

questions.prompt: For `compareTo`, a negative result means that this object comes ___ the compared object in the ordering.
questions.explanation: The sign is what matters: negative means before, 0 means equal according to the ordering, and positive means after.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about interfaces; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: An interface cannot have instance fields or constructors.
An interface method without a body is implicitly `public abstract`.
Every interface method must be abstract.
Interface fields are implicitly `public static final`.

questions.explanation: Interfaces can also have `default`, `static`, and private methods with bodies. They cannot have instance fields or constructors.

questions.prompt: How do you call a static method of an interface?

options.text: Only through an instance of the implementing class.
Through the name of any implementing class.
Through the interface name, for example `ValueComparable.compare(x, y)`.

questions.explanation: A static interface method belongs to the interface itself. Implementing classes do not inherit it.

questions.prompt: `Cloneable` declares a method `clone()`.
questions.explanation: `Cloneable` is a marker interface with no method declaration of its own. Another interface can explicitly require a public copy operation.

questions.prompt: What relationship does the dashed line between `OrderedRational` and `ValueComparable` represent?

context.caption: Relationship between a class and an interface

options.text: The two types are not connected.

questions.explanation: In a UML class diagram, a dashed line indicates that a class implements an interface. A solid inheritance line represents class inheritance.

questions.prompt: A `default` method in an interface has a method body and provides a finished, ___ instance method.
questions.explanation: A `default` method provides an inheritable implementation. A class can override this method.

questions.prompt: Compare the fractions $\frac{5}{8}$ and $\frac{2}{3}$ using cross-products. What does `compareTo` return when the smaller fraction is compared?

options.text: The denominators are positive, so comparison is not possible.

questions.explanation: The cross-products are $5\cdot3=15$ and $8\cdot2=16$. Since 15 is less than 16, $\frac{5}{8}$ comes before the other fraction, and `compareTo` returns a negative value, here -1.

questions.prompt: Which declaration can a class with one superclass and two interfaces use?

options.text: `class C extends I1 implements A, I2`
`class C implements A extends I1, I2`
`class C extends A implements I1, I2`
`class C extends A, B implements I1`

questions.explanation: A class can extend one direct superclass and implement multiple interfaces. The class cannot list two superclasses in `extends`.

questions.prompt: Suppose `OrderedRational` implements `ValueComparable`, which declares `compareTo` and a static method `compare`. `OrderedRational` also provides `numerator()`. `ValueComparable x` and `ValueComparable y` are declared. Select all calls that are possible through `x` or through the interface name; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `OrderedRational.compare(x, y)` as an inherited static method

questions.explanation: The static type `ValueComparable` allows access to its instance method `compareTo`. The static interface method is called through the interface name; `numerator()` is not visible through this reference type.

questions.prompt: A class can extend one direct superclass and implement multiple interfaces.
questions.explanation: Java allows one direct class superclass, but multiple interfaces after `implements`.

questions.prompt: A class implementing an interface method that has no body must declare it with `___` visibility.
questions.explanation: An interface method without a body is `public abstract`. Its implementation cannot restrict its visibility.

options.text: Compiler error: the conflict is unresolved.

questions.explanation: The class resolves the conflict with its own override and explicitly calls `LeftDefault.super.meth()` inside it. Therefore, `A` is printed.

questions.prompt: The expression tree `Addition(Const(4), Neg(Addition(Const(1), Const(2))))` is given. `Addition` has two child nodes, `Neg` has one, and `Const` has none. Count each node exactly once. How many nodes does the tree contain?
questions.explanation: The tree contains the outer addition, `Const(4)`, the negation, an inner addition, and two more constants: $1+1+1+1+2=6$ nodes in total.

questions.prompt: Select all correct rules for interface `default` methods; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: For two unrelated defaults with the same signature, the class must resolve the conflict.
A default from a more specific interface takes precedence over a more general inherited default.
An interface default always takes precedence over a class method.
An inherited concrete class method takes precedence over an interface default.

questions.explanation: The precedence rules account for concrete class methods and interface specificity. Two unrelated, conflicting defaults cannot be selected automatically.

questions.prompt: In a cache, `value == 0` can reliably indicate that `evaluate()` has never been executed.
questions.explanation: 0 can be a valid result. Therefore, the cache needs a separate flag such as `evaluated`.

questions.prompt: An interface contains `private String label()` and a `default` method that calls `label()`. What must an implementing class provide?

options.text: Only the required abstract interface methods, not `label()`.

questions.explanation: The private method is an internal implementation detail of the interface. The class does not have to implement it; it only has to fulfill the public contract.
The final reference `VALUES` cannot be reassigned, but its array element can be changed. `size()` is a static interface method and is therefore called as `Settings.size()`; `App` does not inherit it.

questions.prompt: A class has no inherited concrete class method. A more specific interface overrides an inherited default. Which branch of the flow determines the method call?

context.caption: Precedence rules for inherited methods

options.text: The class must override the conflict in every case.
The first default alphabetically is always used.
The inherited class method is used.
The more specific default is used.

questions.explanation: If no concrete class method takes precedence, a default from a more specific interface takes precedence over the more general inherited default.

options.text: Compiler error due to the assignment to `long`

questions.explanation: In the first expression, the values are widened to `long` before multiplication. In the second, an overflowed `int` is produced first; the later cast cannot restore the lost value.

questions.prompt: The sealed abstract class `Expression` permits exactly `Const`, `Neg`, and `Addition` as concrete subclasses. A pattern-matching `switch` has one case for each of these three types. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The `switch` is not exhaustive because abstract classes always require a `default` case.
The switch is exhaustive and does not need a `default` case.
The `switch` is exhaustive only if `Expression` can be instantiated.
A `default` case is required because `sealed` does not restrict subclasses.

questions.explanation: The sealed hierarchy restricts the permitted cases. If the `switch` handles every permitted concrete subclass, it is exhaustive.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about `Cloneable` and `Countable`; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `Cloneable` requires a public `clone()` implementation in every implementing class.
`Cloneable` marks a property but does not itself declare a `clone()` method.
An interface such as `Countable` can explicitly declare `Object clone()` as part of its contract.
A marker interface must contain at least one abstract method.

questions.explanation: `Cloneable` is a marker with no methods of its own. `Countable` can independently require a public `clone()` operation.

questions.prompt: Two different fraction objects return 0 from `compareTo`. What follows from this?

options.text: They are equal according to the comparison ordering, but need not be the same reference.
`compareTo` is implemented incorrectly because it must return `-1` or `1`.

questions.explanation: `compareTo` describes equality according to the implemented ordering. Reference identity is checked separately with `==`.

questions.prompt: `final` and `sealed` have the same effect: both permit only explicitly listed subclasses.
questions.explanation: `final` prohibits all subclasses. `sealed` selectively permits specified direct subclasses.

questions.prompt: An interface `Described` declares `String description()` and provides `default void printDescription()`. Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The class can inherit the finished `printDescription()` method.
The method `description()` is automatically replaced by the default.
A concrete implementing class must provide `description()`.

questions.explanation: The interface requires `description()` and provides a default implementation for `printDescription()`. This method can be inherited or overridden.

questions.prompt: Which multiplication avoids an `int` overflow with `int` operands before storing the result in `long`?
questions.explanation: The cast must happen before multiplication so that the multiplication itself is performed as `long`. A later cast cannot undo an earlier `int` overflow.

questions.prompt: Several expression nodes should share the same cache and `getValue()` logic, but define their computations differently in `evaluate()`. Which design fits?

options.text: A static method with no subclasses.
An interface with a shared instance field for the cache.
A final class from which all node types inherit.
An abstract class with shared state and an abstract `evaluate()` method.

questions.explanation: The cache fields and `getValue()` are shared state and shared code. An abstract method lets each concrete node type provide its own computation.

questions.prompt: `abstract sealed class Expression permits Const, Neg, Addition` has exactly these permitted direct subclasses. A `switch` handles `Const`, `Neg`, and `Addition`. Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Any other class may inherit directly from `Expression`.
The `switch` covers all permitted cases and can be exhaustive.

questions.explanation: `abstract` prevents direct instantiation, `sealed` restricts direct subclasses, and the three cases cover all permitted concrete variants.

options.text: Compiler error due to the default method

questions.explanation: An inherited concrete class method takes precedence over interface defaults. Therefore, `Concrete.meth()` runs and `C` is printed.

questions.prompt: Compare $\frac{50000}{50001}$ with $\frac{50001}{50000}$ using cross-products. The denominators are positive, and the products are calculated as `long`. What is the sign of `compareTo`?

options.text: The comparison is impossible because the numbers are too large.

questions.explanation: The cross-products are 2 500 000 000 and 2 500 100 001. The first is smaller, so the comparison is negative; casting before multiplication prevents an `int` overflow.

questions.prompt: Which Java declaration matches the two relationships shown in the diagram?

context.caption: A class extends a superclass and implements an interface

questions.explanation: The solid line shows class inheritance, expressed with `extends`. The dashed line shows interface implementation, expressed with `implements`.

questions.prompt: A reference `e` has static type `Expression` and points to an object of class `Const`. `Expression.getValue()` calls `evaluate()`; `Const` overrides `evaluate()` and returns 8. Which implementation runs?

options.text: An implementation in `Expression`, because the static type determines it.
None; abstract methods cannot be called dynamically.
`Const.evaluate()`, because the object's runtime class determines it.

questions.explanation: The static type permits the call to `getValue()`. The inner call to the overridden instance method is dynamically bound to `Const.evaluate()`.

questions.prompt: Two different fraction objects `a` and `b` return `a.compareTo(b) == 0`. This implies that `a == b` is true.
questions.explanation: `compareTo` can indicate equality according to the ordering without both variables referring to the same object. For references, `==` checks identity.
`a` and `b` point to the same array. `final` only prevents reassignment of `a`, so `a[0]` sees the change made through `b`.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about resolving interface defaults; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: A more specific interface can replace a more general inherited default.
A concrete class method takes precedence over a default.
When two defaults conflict, Java always chooses the interface listed first.
When two unrelated defaults conflict, the class must override the method.

questions.explanation: The first three statements match the precedence rules. The order of the interfaces in `implements` does not resolve a conflict automatically.

questions.prompt: A class can implement an interface method using `protected` even though the method is implicitly `public abstract` in the interface.
questions.explanation: The implementation cannot restrict the visibility of the public interface contract. It must therefore be `public`.

questions.prompt: An expression tree is `Addition(Neg(Const(8)), Const(16))`. `Const(x)` returns $x$, `Neg(a)` returns the negation of its child's value, and `Addition(l,r)` adds its children's values. What value does the tree compute?
questions.explanation: `Neg(Const(8))` evaluates to -8. The addition then computes $-8+16=8$.

questions.prompt: You are developing a role-playing game: mages and warriors both store health points and share the same `takeDamage()` logic. Their `attack()` method differs. Which Java structure fits best?

options.text: An abstract superclass with health points, a shared `takeDamage()` method, and an abstract `attack()` method
Two independent classes that duplicate the same code
A `final` superclass inherited by mages and warriors
An interface with an instance field `health` and a constructor

questions.explanation: The abstract superclass can provide the shared state and `takeDamage()`. The subclasses each add their own `attack()` implementation.

questions.prompt: Your university app sorts exams and assignment deadlines. The classes have no shared state or domain superclass, but should offer the same sorting capability. `compareTo` returns a negative value if this object should come before the other, `0` if they are equal in the ordering, and a positive value if it should come after. Which structure fits best?

options.text: An interface with the `compareTo` contract, implemented by both classes
A static method inherited by both classes
A `final` class that replaces both classes
A shared abstract class, solely so both classes inherit the same sorting method

questions.explanation: An interface is suitable when different classes should offer the same capability without sharing state. The sign of `compareTo` describes the ordering.

questions.prompt: Your banking app has a `PinValidator` contract for four-digit PINs. Each digit can be from 0 to 9; leading zeros are allowed. How many different inputs can the validator receive?
questions.explanation: Each of the four positions has 10 possibilities. There are 10⁴ = 10,000 inputs in total; the interface contract does not change this input space.

questions.prompt: A navigation app has a variable of type `RouteMode` that points to a `BikeMode` object. `BikeMode` overrides `RouteMode.route()`. What does the call `mode.route()` return?

context.caption: The subclass overrides the instance method.

options.text: The call causes a compiler error
Both strings are returned one after the other

questions.explanation: For an overridden instance method, the actual object at runtime determines which implementation runs. Therefore, `BikeMode.route()` runs here.

questions.prompt: You have a `final` variable that always points to the same array. Can the app still change a number stored inside that array?
questions.explanation: `final` prevents the variable from being assigned a different array. The contents of the referenced array can still change.

questions.prompt: You are testing the expression tree `Add(Neg(Const(5)), Add(Const(3), Const(4)))`. `Const(n)` stores a number, `Neg(x)` negates its child, and `Add(x, y)` adds its children. Each node object runs `evaluate()` exactly once on the first `getValue()` call and caches the result; each node here is a separate object. You call `getValue()` twice on the root. How many `evaluate()` calls occur in total?
questions.explanation: The tree has six nodes. On the first call, each node is evaluated once; the second call returns the root's cached result. Thus, there are six calls in total.

questions.prompt: Assume Java 21 for this question. An expression tree has an abstract base class `Expr` and exactly two direct subclasses: `NumberNode` and `PlusNode`. Both subclasses are `final`. The `switch` must handle all values of type `Expr` and be exhaustive as a switch expression without `default`. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: `Expr` is `final`, and `NumberNode` and `PlusNode` inherit from it.
`Expr` is an ordinary abstract class with any number of subclasses; the `switch` contains only a case for `NumberNode`.
`Expr` is `sealed` and permits exactly `NumberNode` and `PlusNode` with `permits`; the `switch` has one type-pattern case for each class.

questions.explanation: `sealed` with `permits` restricts the direct subclasses. Since both permitted subclasses are `final`, type-pattern cases for both cover every possible `Expr` value, making the switch expression exhaustive.

questions.prompt: A plugin may independently implement any selection of eight optional interfaces; no selection is excluded. How many different combinations of these capabilities are possible?
questions.explanation: Each of the eight interfaces can either be implemented or omitted. This gives 2⁸ = 256 possible combinations.

questions.prompt: An export module implements two unrelated interfaces that both provide a `default` method `reset()` with their own method bodies. The class compiles unambiguously without its own `reset()` because Java automatically selects one of the interfaces. Is this correct?
questions.explanation: There is no automatic selection between two unrelated, conflicting defaults. The implementing class must override `reset()` itself to resolve the conflict.

questions.prompt: A plugin inherits from `BasePanel`, whose concrete method `render()` returns the text `base`. It also implements `PanelStyle`, which provides a `default render()` with the text `default`. What text does `panel.render()` produce?

options.text: The call is impossible because of a conflict
The variable's static type determines which of the two texts is returned

questions.explanation: An inherited concrete class method takes precedence over an interface `default` method with the same name.
